{{short description|Sentence that resists simple formalization}}

In [[semantics]], a '''donkey sentence''' is a sentence containing a [[pronoun]] which is semantically [[Bound variable pronoun|bound]] but syntactically free. They are a classic puzzle in [[formal semantics (natural language)|formal semantics]] and [[philosophy of language]] because they are fully [[Grammaticality|grammatical]] and yet defy straightforward attempts to generate their [[formal language]] equivalents. In order to explain how speakers are able to understand them, semanticists have proposed a variety of formalisms including systems of [[dynamic semantics]] such as [[Discourse representation theory]]. Their name comes from the example sentence "Every farmer who owns a donkey beats it", in which "it" acts as '''a donkey pronoun''' because it is semantically but not syntactically bound by the indefinite [[noun phrase]] "a donkey". The phenomenon is known as '''donkey anaphora'''.{{efn|Emar Maier describes donkey pronouns as "bound but not [[c-command]]ed" in a [[Linguist List]] [https://linguistlist.org/issues/17/17-3393/ review] of Paul D. Elbourne's ''Situations and Individuals'' ([[MIT Press]], 2006).<ref>{{cite journal |type=review|last1=Maier |first1=Emar |title=Situations and Individuals by Paul D. Elbourne |journal=LINGUIST List |date=20 Nov 2006 |volume=17 |issue=3393 |url=https://linguistlist.org/issues/17/17-3393/}}</ref> [[Chris Barker (linguist)|Barker]] and Shan define a donkey pronoun as "a pronoun that lies outside the restrictor of a [[Quantification (linguistics)|quantifier]] or the if-clause of a [[Conditional clause|conditional]], yet [[covariance|covaries]] with some [[Quantification (linguistics)|quantification]]al element inside it, usually an [[indefinite article|indefinite]]."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Barker |first1=Chris |last2=Shan |first2=Chung-chieh |author-link1=Chris Barker (linguist)|title=Donkey anaphora is in-scope binding |journal=Semantics and Pragmatics |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=1–46 |date=9 June 2008|doi=10.3765/sp.1.1 |url=https://semprag.org/index.php/sp/article/view/sp.1.1/74 |access-date=29 December 2020 |issn=1937-8912|doi-access=free }}</ref>}}

== Examples ==

The following sentences are examples of donkey sentences.
*{{lang|la|Omne homo habens asinum videt illum.}} ("Every man who owns a donkey sees it.") — [[Walter Burley]] (1328), {{lang|la|De puritate artis logicae tractatus longior}}<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EYCSacIK_-EC|title=De puritate artis logicae tractatus longior|author=Gualterus Burlaeus|publisher=Meiner Verlag|date=1988|isbn=9783787307173}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3_1snsgmqU8C&pg=PA269|title=Concise Encyclopedia of Semantics|author=Keith Allan|author-link=Keith Allan (linguist)|publisher=Elsevier|date=2010|isbn=9780080959696}}</ref>
*Every farmer who owns a donkey beats it.<ref name="Geach">{{cite book|title=Reference and Generality|author=Peter Geach|date=1962|author-link=Peter Geach|via=philosophieweb0.001.free.fr/GeachRandG.pdf|publisher=Cornell University Press|location=Ithaca and London}}</ref>
*If a farmer owns a donkey, he beats it.
*Every police officer who arrested a murderer insulted him.

==Analysis of donkey sentences==
The goal of [[formal semantics (natural language)|formal semantics]] is to show how sentences of a [[natural language]] such as [[English language|English]] could be translated into a formal logical language, and so would then be amenable to mathematical analysis. Following [[Bertrand Russell|Russell]], it is typical to translate [[definiteness|indefinite noun phrases]] using an [[existential quantifier]],<ref name="HeimDiss">{{cite thesis|last=Heim|first=Irene|author-link=Irene Heim|date=1982|title=The Semantics of Definite and Indefinite Noun Phrases|type=PhD|publisher=University of Massachusetts Amherst|url=https://semanticsarchive.net/Archive/jA2YTJmN/Heim%20Dissertation%20with%20Hyperlinks.pdf|pages=11–12|access-date=29 December 2020}}</ref>
as in the following simple example from Burchardt ''et al'':

: "A woman smokes." is translated as <math>  \exists x \,( \text{WOMAN}(x) \land \text{SMOKES}(x))</math><ref name="Saarland1">{{cite web |last1=Burchardt |first1=Aljoscha |last2=Walter |first2=Stephan |last3=Koller |first3=Alexander |last4=Kohlhase |first4=Michael |last5=Blackburn |first5=Patrick |last6=Bos |first6=Johan |author-link4=Michael Kohlhase|title=Anaphoric Pronouns |url=http://www.coli.uni-saarland.de/projects/milca/courses/comsem/html/node207.html#sec_drt.anapron |website=Computational Semantics 11.1.1 |publisher=Saarland University |access-date=29 December 2020}}</ref>

The prototypical donkey sentence, "Every farmer who owns a donkey beats it.", requires careful consideration for adequate description (though reading "each" in place of "every" does simplify the formal analysis). The donkey pronoun in this case is the word ''it''. Correctly translating this sentence will require using a [[universal quantifier]] for the indefinite noun phrase "a donkey", rather than the expected existential quantifier.

The naive first attempt at translation given below is not a well-formed sentence, since the variable <math> y </math> is left [[Free variables and bound variables|free]] in the predicate <math> \text{BEAT}(x,y) </math>.<ref name="Saarland2" />

: <math>  \forall x\, (\text{FARMER} (x) \land \exists y \,( \text{DONKEY}(y) \land \text{OWNS}(x,y)) \rightarrow \text{BEAT}(x,y)) </math>

It may be attempted to extend the [[Scope (logic)|scope]] of the existential quantifier to bind the free instance of <math> y </math>, but it still does not give a correct translation.<ref name="Saarland2">{{cite web |last1=Burchardt |first1=Aljoscha |last2=Walter |first2=Stephan |last3=Koller |first3=Alexander |last4=Kohlhase |first4=Michael |last5=Blackburn |first5=Patrick |last6=Bos |first6=Johan |title=Donkey Sentences |url=http://www.coli.uni-saarland.de/projects/milca/courses/comsem/html/node208.html |website=Computational Semantics 11.1.2 |publisher=Saarland University |access-date=29 December 2020}}</ref>

: <math>  \forall x \,\exists y\, (\text{FARMER} (x) \land \text{DONKEY}(y) \land \text{OWNS}(x,y) \rightarrow \text{BEAT}(x,y)) </math>

This translation is incorrect since it is already true if there exists any object that is not a donkey: Given any object to be substituted for <math> x </math>, substituting any non-donkey object for <math> y </math> makes the [[material conditional]] true (since its [[antecedent (logic)|antecedent]] is false), and so existential clause is true for every choice of <math> x </math>.

A correct translation into first-order logic for the donkey sentence seems to be

: <math>  \forall x\, \forall y\, ((\text{FARMER} (x) \land \text{DONKEY}(y) \land \text{OWNS}(x,y)) \rightarrow \text{BEAT}(x,y)) </math>,

indicating that indefinites must sometimes be interpreted as existential quantifiers, and other times as universal quantifiers.<ref name="Saarland2" />

There is nothing wrong with donkey sentences: they are grammatically correct, they are well-formed and meaningful, and their syntax is regular. However, it is difficult to explain how donkey sentences produce their semantic results, and how those results generalize consistently with all other language use. If such an analysis were successful, it might allow a computer program to accurately translate natural language forms into [[logical form]].<ref name="Knott">{{cite journal |last1=Knott |first1=Alistair |title=An Algorithmic Framework for Specifying the Semantics of Discourse Relations |journal=Computational Intelligence |date=2000 |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=501–510 |doi=10.1111/0824-7935.00123 |s2cid=1295252 |url=http://www.cs.otago.ac.nz/staffpriv/alik/papers/cirevision.pdf}}</ref> It is unknown how natural language users agree – apparently effortlessly – on the meaning of sentences such as the examples.{{Citation needed|date=January 2021}}

There may be several equivalent ways of describing this process. In fact, [[Hans Kamp]] (1981) and [[Irene Heim]] (1982) independently proposed very similar accounts in different terminology, which they called [[discourse representation theory]] (DRT) and [[file change semantics]] (FCS), respectively.

==Theories of donkey anaphora==
It is usual to distinguish two main kinds of theories about the semantics of donkey pronouns. The most classical proposals fall within the so-called ''description-theoretic approach'', a label that is meant to encompass all the theories that treat the semantics of these pronouns as akin to, or derivative from, the semantics of [[definite descriptions]]. The second main family of proposals goes by the name ''dynamic theories'', and they model donkey anaphora – and anaphora in general – on the assumption that the meaning of a sentence lies in its potential to change the context (understood as the information shared by the participants in a conversation).<ref>{{cite book|last= Elbourne|first=Paul|title=Situations and individuals|year=2005|publisher=MIT Press|isbn=9780262550611}}</ref>

===Description-theoretic approaches===
{{expand section|date=March 2020}}
Description-theoretic approaches are theories of donkey pronouns in which definite descriptions play an important role. They were pioneered by [[Gareth Evans (philosopher)|Gareth Evans]]'s E-type approach,<ref name="Evans" /> which holds that donkey pronouns can be understood as referring terms whose reference is fixed by description.

For example, in "Every farmer who owns a donkey beats it.", the donkey pronoun "it" can be expanded as a definite description to yield "Every farmer who owns a donkey beats the donkey he/she owns." This expanded sentence can be interpreted along the lines of Russell's [[theory of descriptions]].<ref name="Partee">{{cite web |last1=Partee |first1=Barbara H. |author1-link=Barbara Partee |title=Formal Semantics and Current Problems of Semantics, Lecture 6. Kamp-Heim I. Anaphora with Indefinite Antecedents; Donkey Anaphora |url=https://people.umass.edu/partee/720_09/materials/720_09_2-Heim1.pdf |website=RGGU: Formal Semantics and Anaphora |publisher=University of Massachusetts |access-date=29 December 2020 |page=9 |date=18 March 2008}}</ref>

Later authors have attributed an even larger role to definite descriptions, to the point of arguing that donkey pronouns have the semantics,<ref>{{cite book|last= Cooper|first=Robin|chapter=The interpretation of pronouns|title=Syntax and Semantics 10: Selections from the third Gröningen roundtable|year=1979|publisher=Academic Press|editor1=Frank Heny|editor2=Helmut Schnelle|isbn=012613510X}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last= Neale|first=Stephen|author-link=Stephen Neale|title=Descriptions|year=1990|publisher=The MIT Press|isbn=0262640317}}</ref> and even the syntax,<ref>{{cite book|last1= Heim|first1=Irene|last2= Kratzer|first2=Angelika|author-link1=Irene Heim|author-link2=Angelika Kratzer|title=Semantics in Generative Grammar|year=1998|publisher=Blackwell|isbn=0631197133}}</ref> of definite descriptions. Approaches of the latter kind are usually called ''D-type''.

===Discourse representation theory===
{{More citations needed section|date=January 2023}}
Donkey sentences became a major force in advancing [[semantics|semantic]] research in the 1980s, with the introduction of [[discourse representation theory]] (DRT). During that time, an effort was made to settle the inconsistencies which arose from the attempts to translate donkey sentences into [[first-order logic]].

The solution that [[Discourse representation theory|DRT]] provides for the donkey sentence problem can be roughly outlined as follows: The common semantic function of non-anaphoric [[noun phrase]]s is the introduction of a new [[discourse referent]], which is in turn available for the binding of anaphoric expressions. No quantifiers are introduced into the representation, thus overcoming the scope problem that the logical translations had.

===Dynamic Predicate Logic===
{{expand section|date=March 2020}}
Dynamic Predicate Logic models pronouns as [[first-order logic]] [[Variable (mathematics)|variables]], but allows quantifiers in a [[Well-formed formula|formula]] to bind variables in other formulae.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Groenendijk|first1=Jeroen|last2=Stokhof|first2=Martin|author-link1=Jeroen Groenendijk|author-link2=Martin Stokhof|date=1991|title=Dynamic Predicate Logic|journal=Linguistics and Philosophy|language=en|volume=14|pages=39–100|doi=10.1007/BF00628304|s2cid=62551132|url=https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/1971390/27375_dpl.pdf}}</ref>

==History==
[[Walter Burley]], a medieval scholastic philosopher, introduced donkey sentences in the context of ''[[supposition theory]]'', the medieval equivalent of reference theory.

[[Peter Geach]] reintroduced donkey sentences as a [[counterexample]] to [[Richard Montague]]'s proposal for a generalized formal representation of [[Quantification (linguistics)|quantification]] in [[natural language]].<ref name="Geach" /> His example was reused by [[David Kellogg Lewis|David Lewis]] (1975),<ref name="Lewis1">{{cite encyclopedia |last1=Lewis |first1=David |author1-link=David Lewis (philosopher) |editor1-last=Keenan |editor1-first=Edward L. |encyclopedia=Formal Semantics of Natural Language |date=1975 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=9780511897696 |title=Adverbs of quantification|via=users.ox.ac.uk/~sfop0776/LewisQA.pdf}}</ref> [[Gareth Evans (philosopher)|Gareth Evans]] (1977)<ref name="Evans">{{Cite journal|last=Evans|first=Gareth|date=September 1977|title=Pronouns, Quantifiers and Relative Clauses (I)|journal=Canadian Journal of Philosophy|language=en|volume=7|issue=3|pages=467–536|doi=10.1080/00455091.1977.10717030|s2cid=146125231 }}</ref> and many others, and is still quoted in recent publications.
